html:
In 1923 an American expedition led by Roy Chapman Andrews of the American Museum of Natural History found the first nests of dinosaur eggs known to science, at the Flaming Cliffs (Bayanzag) in the Gobi Desert of southern Mongolia. Andrews named the cliffs for their red and orange sandstone, which glows at sunset.

His Central Asiatic Expeditions of 1922 to 1930 travelled by car, with camel caravans carrying fuel and supplies. They set out to find early humans in Asia and found none, but the rocks, about 75 million years old, held superb fossils: Protoceratops, small early mammals, the eggs, and the first Velociraptor, named in 1924. The eggs were thought to be Protoceratops eggs, so a toothless dinosaur found on a nest was named Oviraptor, "egg thief". In the 1990s new finds showed the eggs were its own, and it had been brooding them.

The finds made Andrews famous, and he is often named as a model for Indiana Jones. Political trouble in Mongolia and China ended the expeditions in 1930. Later Soviet, Polish and Mongolian teams kept digging, and the smuggling of Gobi fossils is still a problem.
